# Fabricated and inaccurate citations generated by large language models for biomedical topics: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Raphael Malikian. Independent researcher, Palmdale, CA, USA. ORCID 0009-0008-4326-4205. rtmalikian@gmail.com.

Condensed version for the Journal of the Medical Library Association (Knowledge Synthesis). The full Cochrane order version, with complete methods, appendices and characteristics tables, is the preprint and repository version (manuscript.md in the review repository). No number differs between the two versions. This cut carries the corrected version's numbers (robustness pass, 23 October 2026): the first version's condensed cut reported 25 experiments with 18.6% fabricated and 29.4% fully accurate; those figures are superseded.

## Abstract (structured, under 250 words)

Objective: to pool, from generation experiments, the proportions of LLM generated biomedical references that are completely fabricated, that carry any major inaccuracy, and that are fully accurate. Methods: PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAIRE and Crossref were searched on 22 October 2026, with citation chasing and full re-adjudication in a robustness pass on 23 October 2026 (16,474 records screened in total). Eligible studies prompted LLMs to generate biomedical references, reported the count generated, and verified each reference against a named source. An adapted risk of bias tool was specified before extraction. Random effects meta-analysis of proportions (logit, REML) kept model arms visible, with per study sensitivity pools and GRADE adapted for proportions. Results: 63 experiments (148 arms) and one published literature audit (separate stratum) were included. Completely fabricated: pooled 19.4% (95% CI 14.9 to 24.8; 113 arms; 22,461 references; I squared 97.1%). Fully accurate: 37.0% (27.2 to 47.9; 58 arms; 14,224 references). Any major inaccuracy: 16.5% (5.7 to 39.2; 20 arms, 14 studies). Arms with retrieval or browsing active pooled 5.8% fabricated against 31.0% with retrieval off (26 retrieval arms). All critical outcomes were rated very low certainty. Conclusions: about one generated biomedical reference in five did not exist, and just over one in three was fully accurate. Verification of every generated reference against a database is the step this literature supports.

## Introduction

A reference list tells a reader that a paper exists and can be checked. Large language models produce lists that keep that shape and break the content: plausible authors, a real journal, a fitting year, and no such article, or a real article with a wrong title or a DOI that resolves elsewhere. Single studies have reported fabrication from 1 in 150 references for one current model (Adiguzel 2026) to 98 in 149 for another (UcarGundogar 2026). Editors, reviewers and librarians have had no pooled figure to argue from. Audits of the published literature show why the question has moved: Yin 2026 estimated about 146,932 non-existent references across 2.5 million papers in 2025, and Topaz 2026 counted fabricated references in about 1 in 277 published biomedical papers in early 2026, up from about 1 in 2,828 in 2023. Those audits measure what reached print. This review measures the generation step, pooling experiments on their shared denominator, references generated.

## Methods

Eligibility, outcomes and analysis followed a protocol written before screening (version 1.0, 22 October 2026), reported in full in the repository version. Definitions: completely fabricated, no matching publication exists; major inaccuracy, an error that prevents retrieval or misattributes the source, including fabricated; fully accurate, every checked field correct. A study entered a pool only where its printed definition mapped exactly, with the mapping logged per row. Large scale audits of published literature formed a separate stratum and were never pooled with generation experiments.

Search: PubMed (372 retrieved), Europe PMC (14,090, broad string, logged), OpenAIRE (10), Crossref (1,000 retrieved per query; its total-results figures are relevance match counts, not result sets), OpenAlex test page (25). arXiv and Semantic Scholar were attempted and blocked by rate limits and are logged as blocked. Embase, Scopus and Web of Science strings are prepared and marked run pending access; they were not searched.

Selection and extraction: two LLM screeners with different written rules screened 15,985 deduplicated records apart (agreement 94.29%; Cohen kappa 0.13, a prevalence effect reported in the team log); in the first version a coded adjudication rule passed 122 reports to full text, and in the robustness pass every screening disagreement was re-adjudicated by reading and systematic citation chasing added 489 records and 2 studies, taking the included set to 63 generation studies. Extraction captured 57 fields per study and per model arm, values exactly as printed; the robustness pass added a second, fully independent extraction of every study, compared field by field against the first, with every discrepancy settled by re-reading the source and logged (robustness-discrepancy-log.md). Risk of bias used an adapted eight domain tool specified before extraction (topic and prompt sampling, model and prompt reporting, generation settings, verification source, verifier independence, duplicate or blinded verification, partial match handling, selective reporting), applied by two assessors apart and adjudicated by reading the paper and both rationales in the corrected version (the first version took the more cautious judgement). It is an adapted tool, not RoB 2 or QUADAS-2. Synthesis: random effects meta-analysis of proportions in Python, logit transformation, REML tau squared, prediction intervals at 10 or more arms, pre-specified subgroups (model family, retrieval, publication type, list length where printed, model year), and sensitivity pools per study, without preprints, leaving one family out, and at low or some concerns risk of bias only. No PROSPERO number was issued before analysis; a PROSPERO-ready form was prepared before screening and the OSF record is the parallel route. Nothing is backdated; the robustness pass is dated after first publication and the amendment is logged in the protocol.

## Results

Flow: 16,497 records retrieved from databases plus 979 citation chasing candidates (489 new), 16,474 screened in total, 16,181 excluded at title and abstract, 293 reports sought, 115 not retrieved, 178 assessed, 111 excluded with one reason each, 66 generation reports covering 63 unique studies included, plus 1 audit report. The 63 studies ran from 2023 to 2026 across radiology, orthopaedics, dentistry, neurocritical care, mental health, ophthalmology and other fields, and contributed 148 model arms.

Risk of bias: high in 30 studies, some concerns in 33, low in none. Verification conduct drove the judgements: many studies never stated who checked the references, whether the checker knew which model produced them, or whether checking was duplicated.

Completely fabricated: pooled 19.4% (95% CI 14.9 to 24.8), 113 arms, 50 studies, 4,716 of 22,461 references, tau squared 2.59, I squared 97.1%, prediction interval 1.0 to 85.6%. Per study pool 24.7% (18.2 to 32.5). Without preprints 19.8%. At low or some concerns risk of bias only, 19.1%.

Any major inaccuracy: pooled 16.5% (5.7 to 39.2), 20 arms, 14 studies, 562 of 2,668 references, I squared 96.7%. The first version's 36.0% rested on counts that settlement found did not map to the definition and should not be quoted; even corrected, the pool is thin and is read that way.

Fully accurate: pooled 37.0% (27.2 to 47.9), 58 arms, 28 studies, 6,089 of 14,224 references, tau squared 2.89, I squared 98.2%, prediction interval 1.9 to 94.8%. Per study pool 38.2% (28.8 to 48.6).

Subgroups: fabricated by family, Claude 5.9% (9 arms), GPT 24.4% (59), Gemini 21.7% (15), DeepSeek 29.6% (10); fully accurate by family, Claude 65.9%, GPT 33.4%, Gemini 23.6%. Family pools mix generations and topics and are reported as descriptions of this literature, not product rankings. With retrieval or browsing active, fabricated pooled 5.8% (26 arms) against 31.0% with retrieval off (50 arms); one study showed the pattern internally, with web search cutting fabrication in the same model family from 82 of 396 to 7 of 296 (Pastucha 2026). List length and model year subgroups were not estimable from what studies printed and are reported as such in the full version. The audit stratum (Yin 2026) is reported apart in the Introduction and Discussion.

GRADE (adapted for proportions): all three critical outcomes very low certainty, downgraded for risk of bias in verification, inconsistency, and indirectness or imprecision as tabled in the full version's summary of findings.

## Discussion

The pooled figures describe a literature, not a product. The prediction interval for fabrication, 1.0 to 85.6%, and the within study range in Gunes 2026 (15 to 291 fabricated of 480 references per model, same topics, same verification) show that fabrication is a property of a setup: model, version, topic and retrieval state together. Exactly two setups among 148 arms produced an error free list, both at the retrieval grounded end of the literature. The retrieval gap is the largest signal in the review, now carried by 26 arms, and is stated as a direction for testing, in line with the 30 to 50% reductions reported by the mitigation review of Basu and Huynh, and not as a settled effect.

For library practice, the operational reading is plain. A generated reference list is unverified text until each entry has been checked against a database, and the people who run that check at scale are librarians and research support staff. Journals that ask authors to declare AI use could ask how each AI assisted reference was verified, and by whom, at the same time.

Limitations are substantial and are stated in full in the repository version. No study reached low risk of bias; heterogeneity stayed above 95% in every pool; definitions of fabrication differed between studies within stated mapping rules; 115 reports that passed screening were never retrieved, so the included set is the open access visible part of the field; screening and extraction were carried out by an LLM team under a single accountable human author rather than by two human reviewers; and the search could not include Embase, Scopus or Web of Science, nor complete full OpenAlex retrieval past rate limits. Certainty is very low throughout, and the conclusions are sized to that.

## Conclusions

In these experiments, roughly one LLM generated biomedical reference in five did not exist and just over one in three was fully accurate. Entry by entry verification against a database is the only step the evidence supports without qualification. Future experiments should report verification as a method, print counts per arm with denominators, state retrieval status and model version with the generation date, and treat retrieval as an experimental factor. On a literature that did those things, a repeat of this review could support a stronger rating.
